G. Talhar, App, for the Appellant - State. Mr. Amit P. Ghag, for the Respondents. _______________________________________________________________ Coram: Madhav J. Jamdar, J. Dated: 24 January 2025 Judgment:
texts.facts: 2. In the present Criminal Appeal filed under Section 378(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 ("CrPC") the challenge is to the legality and validity of the Judgment and Order dated 11th December 2002 passed by the learned Chief Judicial Magistrate, Alibag, District - Raigad in Regular Criminal Case No.173 of 1989. The prosecution case is set out in Paragraph Nos.1 and 2 of the impugned Judgment and Order, which reads as under :- The State Of Maharashtra vs Rajendra Prabhakar Kale And Anr on 24 January, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/120445098/ 1 "1. This is Regular Criminal Case No.173/1989 filed by the Food Inspector Shri A. N. Rana against the accused No.1- Rajendra Prabhakar Kale, who is nominee of the accused No.2 firm viz. M/s. Parle Beverages Pvt. Ltd. for the offence under 208-APEAL-813-2003.doc sec.7(v) r.w. rule-40(3), punishable under sec.16(1)(a)(ii) & sec.17, Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as "P.F.A.Act", for the purpose of brevity.) 2. (A) The complainant Mr. A.N. Rana, is a Food Inspector, appointed under Sec.9, P.F.A. Act. As per the case of the complainant accused No.1 is the nominee of the firm- accused No.2 situated at village Vanavali, Tal.: Khalapur, Dist.: Raigad. The complainant has further stated that accused No.2 is a firm named & styled as M/s. Parle Beverages Pvt. Ltd. and engaged in manufacturing for sale, distribution for sale and selling of food articles i.e. "FROOTI ORANGE DRINK" at the said premises. On 16.11.1988 at about 14.00 hours at noon time the complainant alongwith independent witness viz. Tanaji Narayan Thombare and Food Supervisor Shri K.B. Shelar visited the premises of the accused No.2. At the time of his visit to the firm-accused No.2, the accused No.1 was present in the premises of the firm and was looking after the production. The complainant disclosed his identity as food inspector to the accused No.1, and further disclosed his intention of drawing of samples of food articles for the purpose of analysis. The complainant inspected the premises of the factory and noticed that "Frooti Orange Drink" was being manufactured in the premises of the factory. The complainant then demanded and purchased nine(9) packets of 200 mls. of frooti orange drink from the accused No.1. The complainant paid Rs.18.45 ps. as purchase cost of nine(9) packets, and obtained cash memo from the accused No.1. The complainant served notice in form-VI and obtained acknowledgment from the accused No.1. (B) The complainant then divided nine packets of frooti orange drink in three equal parts. The complainant then sealed each part of three packets in separate polythene bag, and after wrapping it in brown paper put wax seal on each sample part. The complainant also pasted slip of local health authority having signature of Assistant Commissioner, Food & Drug Administration, Pen, and obtained signature of the accused, signature of independent witness on each sample part. Complainant also put his signature on each sample part. The complainant then prepared detailed panchanama of drawing of sample, sealing it, etc. in the presence of the independent witness, accused and supervisor Shri Shelar. The complainant served notice to accused No.1 under sec.14-A, P. 208-APEAL-813-2003.doc F. A. Act. (C) On 17.11.1988 the complainant sent one part of sample of frooti orange drink alongwith memorandum in form-VII and forwarding letter dt.17.11.1988 by hand delivery in sealed cover to the Public Analyst, New Bombay, through the Assistant Commissioner, Food & Drug Administration Pen. The complainant also sent in sealed packet specimen impression of seal and covering letter to The State Of Maharashtra vs Rajendra Prabhakar Kale And Anr on 24 January, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/120445098/ 2 the Public Analyst. On 17.11.1988 complainant deposited remaining two sample parts in the office of the Assistant Commissioner, Food & Drug Administration, with covering letter, and one sealed packet containing specimen impression seal. (D) On 17.01.1989 complainant received the report of Public Analyst bearing No.391 of dt.16.12.1988 through the Local Health Authority, Pen. The complainant collected necessary documents from accused No.1 and submitted his report in proforma-A with original necessary documents to the Jt. Commissioner, Food & Drug Administration (Bombay Division) Thane, for necessary consent. The Joint Commissioner, Thane, accorded sanction to prosecute accused vide its consent letter dt.17.10.1989. (E) The complainant, therefore, filed this complaint against the accused Nos.1 & 2 in this court alleging that the accused No.1 being the nominee of the accused No.2-firm on 16.11.1988 have committed an offence by manufacturing and stocking for sale on food article i.e. Frooti Orange Drink containing less quantity of ascorbic acid (Vitamin 'C') than the required quantity as per rule-40(3), and thereby committed an offence of sec.7(v) r.w.rule-40(3), pun. u/sec.16(i)(a) (ii),17, of the P.F.A. Act. The complainant filed this complaint in this court on 06.12.1989 against the accused Nos.1 & 2." 3. It is the submission of learned APP that as per Rule 40(3) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, any fruit and vegetable product alleged to be fortified with vitamin C shall contain not less than 40 mgm of ascorbic acid per 100 gm of the product and as per the Report of the Public Analyst the ascorbic acid found is only 27.0 mg / 208-APEAL-813-2003.doc 100 gms. The said Report is at Exhibit 26. The entire basis of the prosecution case is on the basis of the said Report of the Public Analyst.
texts.arguments: 18. Learned defence counsel has placed his reliance on the decision reported in 1985(II) FAC 88: Nizamuddin Siddikbhai Vs. The State of Maharashtra. Their Lordships of Hon'ble Bombay High Court has held that: "It is imperative in my opinion that the public analyst must find out when a sample falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within prescribed limits of variability whether the said adulterated sample renders it injurious to human health or whether it does not render it injurious to public health. The present report of the Public Analyst Ex-38 is silent on this question and in my opinion such report which is vague and defective cannot form the basis for any conviction." Therefore, in such circumstances and in absence of opinion of public analyst in his report Ex.26 the report can be said to be vague and defective." 5. The Supreme Court in the recent decision in the case of Babu Sahebagouda Rudragoudar v. State of Karnataka 1 in Paragraph Nos.39, 40 and 41 has discussed the legal position concerning approach of the Appellate Court while considering the appeal against acquittal as under: "39. This Court in Rajesh Prasad v. State of Bihar [Rajesh Prasad v. State of Bihar, (2022) 3 SCC 471 : (2022) 2 SCC (Cri) 31] encapsulated the legal position covering the field after considering various earlier judgments and held as below : (SCC pp. 482-83, para 29 "29. After referring to a catena of judgments, this Court culled out the following general principles regarding the 1 (2024) 8 SCC 149 208-APEAL-813-2003.doc powers of the appellate court while dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal in the following words : (Chandrappa case [Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka, (2007) 4 SCC 415 : (2007) 2 SCC (Cri) 325] , SCC p. 432, para 42) '42. From the above decisions, in our considered view, the following general principles regarding powers of the appellate The State Of Maharashtra vs Rajendra Prabhakar Kale And Anr on 24 January, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/120445098/ 4 court while dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal emerge: (1) An appellate court has full power to review, reappreciate and reconsider the evidence upon which the order of acquittal is founded. ( 2) The Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 puts no limitation, restriction or condition on exercise of such power and an appellate court on the evidence before it may reach its own conclusion, both on questions of fact and of law. (3) Various expressions, such as, "substantial and compelling reasons", "good and sufficient grounds", "very strong circumstances", "distorted conclusions", "glaring mistakes", etc. are not intended to curtail extensive powers of an appellate court in an appeal against acquittal. Such phraseologies are more in the nature of "flourishes of language" to emphasise the reluctance of an appellate court to interfere with acquittal than to curtail the power of the court to review the evidence and to come to its own conclusion. (4) An appellate court, however, must bear in mind that in case of acquittal, there is double presumption in favour of the accused. Firstly, the presumption of innocence is available to him under the fundamental principle of criminal jurisprudence that every person shall be presumed to be innocent unless he is proved guilty by a competent court of law. Secondly, the accused having secured his acquittal, the presumption of his innocence is further reinforced, reaffirmed and strengthened by the trial court. 208-APEAL-813-2003.doc ( 5) If two reasonable conclusions are possible on the basis of the evidence on record, the appellate court should not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the trial court.' " 40. Further, in H.D. Sundara v. State of Karnataka [H.D. Sundara v. State of Karnataka, (2023) 9 SCC 581 : (2023) 3 SCC (Cri) 748] this Court summarised the principles governing the exercise of appellate jurisdiction while dealing with an appeal against acquittal under Section 378 CrPC as follows : (SCC p. 584, para 8) "8. ... 8.1. The acquittal of the accused further strengthens the presumption of innocence; 8.2. The appellate court, while hearing an appeal against acquittal, is entitled to reappreciate the oral and documentary evidence; 8.3. The appellate court, while deciding an appeal against acquittal, after reappreciating the evidence, is required to consider whether the view taken by the trial court is a possible view which could have been taken on the basis of the evidence on record. 8.4. If the view taken is a possible view, the appellate court cannot overturn the order of acquittal on the ground that another view was also possible; and 8.5. The appellate The State Of Maharashtra vs Rajendra Prabhakar Kale And Anr on 24 January, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/120445098/ 5 court can interfere with the order of acquittal only if it comes to a finding that the only conclusion which can be recorded on the basis of the evidence on record was that the guilt of the accused was proved beyond a reasonable doubt and no other conclusion was possible." 41. Thus, it is beyond the pale of doubt that the scope of interference by an appellate court for reversing the judgment of acquittal recorded by the trial court in favour of the accused has to be exercised within the four corners of the following principles: 41.1. That the judgment of acquittal suffers from patent perversity; 208-APEAL-813-2003.doc 41.2. That the same is based on a misreading/omission to consider material evidence on record; and 41.3. That no two reasonable views are possible and only the view consistent with the guilt of the accused is possible from the evidence available on record. "
